Senses.Explanation: Pressing a gourd under water pictures a buoyant object that slips, turns, or rises instead of staying fixed under the hand. Masters use the scene both for quick responsive turning and for thoughts or formulas that cannot be held down: the corpus itself calls it lively, rolling, revolving, and impossible to pin to one corner.

Senses.Explanation: To catch the moon in water is to grasp at a reflected appearance that cannot be seized there. Tianyin Yuanxiu says asserting that New Year's teaching exists is catching the moon in water. Chushi Fanqi asks how such catching could occur for one who tolerates no grit in the eye; Zhongfeng Mingben uses it in a verse on verbal learning; Ruibai Mingxue pairs it with trying to pluck a flower from a mirror. Zhuanyu Guanheng calls it wasted effort. Chan records retain the reflection scene and apply it to seeking the matter in an image, formulation, or opposed proposition.

Senses.Explanation: The moon in water is the moon’s visible reflection on a water surface, not another moon that can be taken from the water. The Record of Xiangyan Xixin pictures the moon disk suspended in the blue sky and its round image falling into the ocean; the Records of the Source-Mirror describes the water-moon beside a mirror image and explicitly calls the constructed image provisional rather than real. Zhiyan Liaojue says that the bright moon casts its image over a clear pool while neither water nor moon intends the relation, and then speaks of forgetting both. Hongzhi’s verse retains the image as a moonlit waterscape. A previous temple-name substring has been removed because it names a place, not the reflection.

SearchAliases: sealed so tight not even water passes
Zen sealed so tight not even water passes
Senses.Explanation: The phrase occurs 150 times in 76 allowlisted texts. In the records it regularly describes the impassability of the ancestral gate and places associated with Bodhidharma: "before Shaoshi Peak, not even water passes" (少室峰前，水泄不通) and "under the patriarch's gate, not even water passes" (祖師門下，水泄不通). One address sets it against "the Buddha-work gate, where wind passes and grass bends" (佛事門中，風行草偃). Another makes it one of three eyes: one is watertight and ordinary and initiated cannot be distinguished; one opens the whole earth and the ten directions are unobstructed; one surveys high and low and all kinds look up. The phrase also enters public questioning: "where not even water passes, is there still a way through?" (水泄不通處還有過也無). Thus an ordinary image of a perfect seal becomes a stock Chan description of a gate, peak, command, or point at which passage is challenged.

Senses.Note: Seventy-five exact hits occur in forty-four frozen works. Five independent witnesses include answers, comparison, paired formula, and an explicit negative check.

Senses.Explanation: Water cannot wet it is an imperviousness formula: poured or splashed water fails to adhere. Chan masters use it as an answer about what rain cannot moisten, pair it with wind failing to enter, and then test the supposedly sealed condition rather than treating it as an automatic success. Zhaoqing Daoxian answers that the place universal rain does not moisten is “water cannot wet it.” Beiyuan Tong answers a question about this condition with “dry and bare.” Yuanwu Keqin pairs it with wind not entering and a diamond sword. Yunyan Tansheng gives it as his answer about Yaoshan after extinction. Huqiu Shaolong says that even wind-proof and water-proof composure cannot save itself when inspected.

The water buffalo remains a bovine, but Chan records also make it a name borne by Guishan Lingyou, a label applied to people, a herded case figure, and an explicitly borrowed form for “the different kind.” Guishan says that after death he will become one marked with his monastic name and asks whether it should be called Guishan or a water buffalo (喚作溈山僧又是水牯牛；喚作水牯牛又是溈山僧, “call it Guishan and it is also a water buffalo; call it a water buffalo and it is also Guishan”). Changqing Da’an reports watching one, pulling it from grass, and restraining it from damaging crops until it becomes “the white ox in the open field” (露地白牛). Nanquan Puyuan says Old Teacher Wang has raised one, and elsewhere answers Zhaozhou Congshen’s question by saying that the person who knows-there-is goes to become one at a patron’s house. Zhaozhou calls Hanshan and Shide two water buffaloes. Caoshan Benji explicitly says that earlier people “provisionally borrowed the water buffalo for the different kind” (權借水牯牛為異類) and distinguishes a different kind in affairs from one in words. These uses retain the named animal while putting it into distinct recorded situations.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 1,220 hits in 283 files. The seven curated occurrences span six distinct works and preserve self-naming, herding, teasing, a public answer, an explicit retrospective description, and a test exchange. The text-drawn relation to moving among different kinds does not turn the animal into a second referent.

Senses.Explanation: The water steward is a named monastery office, not the head or source of a stream in these witnesses. Monastic codes list the office among the minor posts alongside the bath, charcoal, furnace, garden, and latrine stewards; one code states its concrete responsibility as heating washing water and arranging the community's basins and towels. The term belongs to the working institutional vocabulary that makes the public hall and resident community possible.

Occurrences.Kwic: 縱然親睹明星現，也是街頭破草鞋。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Recorded Sayings of Weian Deran (松隱唯菴然和尚語錄), Weian Deran says even personally seeing the morning star is street-side worn-out straw sandals.

Occurrences.Kwic: 秪有半隻破草鞋，無底無根亦無對。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Recorded Sayings of Wuchu Daguan (無趣老人語錄), Wuchu Daguan says he has only half a soleless, unmatched worn-out straw sandal.

Senses.Explanation: Worn-out straw sandals are damaged travel footwear fit to discard; Chan speakers make the contemptuous object an answer or comparison for formulations, accomplishments, and lineage emblems that someone is still carrying. Huangbo Xiyun calls the patriarchs' dark purport worn-out straw sandals; Jiashan Shanhui answers 'What is the Way?' with them and says to throw them into the lake. Bajiao Huiqing locates a pair inside the house, Foguo asks what they are worth after the matter is understood, Weian Deran calls even seeing the morning star street-side worn-out sandals, and Wuchu Daguan has half a soleless sandal. These are deployments of the bare worn-out-sandals headword; the different wear-out-the-sandals predicate is routed to family evidence.
